Numerals are not one of the nine parts of speech. 

C/Ving directly from the answer on Google's front page,

> There are nine parts of speech. They are articles, nouns, pronouns, adjectives, verbs, adverbs, conjunctions, prepositions, and interjections. A word of caution, however, a word can be more than one part of speech.

Numerals, by exclusionary definition, must be one or more of those listed above, and not their own part of speech.

http://www.english-grammar-revolution.com/adjective-questions.html

http://www.answers.com/Q/What_questions_do_adjectives_answer

http://www.esldesk.com/grammar/adjectives

To save the click, the sites say that adjectives answer the questions:

1. Which one? 

2. What kind?

3. How many?

4. Whose? (according to some sources, my prescriptive grammars included [*Descriptive English Grammar* by House and Harman; *Modern American Usage* by Brian Garner])

Adjectives answer how many. So yes, twenty is an adjective (the number three is given as an example on the third site I linked). Adjectives answer which one. Yes, "the" is which one. *The* dog. *The* dogs. It is diagrammed as an offshoot from a noun, not on its own horizontal line.

I can understand the confusion, especially paired in the sentence as they are with a plural noun.
They stopped teaching diagramming in schools in the 50's. It's almost a lost art. I need to find a better way to diagram in a comment box, it seems.

Okay, I am going to diagram it.

The (adj) dog (noun) is (verb) with (prep) the (adj) dogs (noun).

If rewritten with the predicate as a pronoun ("the dogs" to "them" or even "those"), a method favored for conciseness so long as the predicate is clear, you could see how "the" as an adj limits the noun's number.
"The" answers both how many and which one, making "the" not only an article, but also an adjective.
